verses.note: The verb for Abel's blood crying out is the same verb Scripture uses for the cry of the powerless whom God hears. The first victim of violence becomes the first voice God attends to on behalf of someone who could not defend himself.
Israel's law later commands that a runaway slave not be returned to a master or oppressed (Deuteronomy 23:15-16). Hagar's story shows why such a law was needed, even in Abram's own house.
The chosen family is marked by righteousness and justice, the very things absent from Sodom (Ezekiel 16:49). The contrast between Abraham's household and Sodom is set up in God's own words.

The law repeatedly names the widow among those God defends (Exodus 22:22, Deuteronomy 10:18). Judah's delay leaves Tamar with neither support nor freedom, and the rest of the chapter turns on the question of who will do right by her.
Joseph's revised plan provides for the hungry households back in Canaan, not only for the men in front of him. Even his testing is bent toward feeding the vulnerable.

The narrative names forced labor as affliction, not as ordinary economics. Israel's law will draw directly on this memory in forbidding the oppression of foreigners and workers (Exodus 22:21; 23:9), since Israel knows from the inside what it is to be the stranger under another's power.

Moses' first recorded act as an adult is to side with the oppressed. His instinct for justice is right, but his method is secret and violent, and the story will show that zeal for justice is not the same as a commission from God.

The gifts function as back wages for generations of unpaid labor, and they fulfill God's word to Abraham that his descendants would come out with great possessions (Genesis 15:14). Israel's law later applies the same principle to every released slave (Deuteronomy 15:13-15).

The foremen appeal to Pharaoh's justice and find none. The scene shows why Israel's cry must finally go to God: those who hold unjust power do not correct themselves, and the oppressed need a judge above the king.

Israel leaves not as runaways with nothing but as laborers paid at last. Later law applies the principle to every released slave, who is not to be sent away empty-handed (Deuteronomy 15:13-15), and it grounds the rule in the memory of Egypt.

The Sabbath is a law of rest for those who could not claim it. Deuteronomy 5:14-15 makes the point explicit, grounding the day in Israel's memory of slavery so that servants may rest as their masters do. No worker, animal, or foreigner is outside its protection.

The command guards what a neighbor needs to live, whether his goods or his own freedom. Paul turns it around into a positive duty: the thief should work so that he can give to those in need (Ephesians 4:28).
Even among the priests, the law insists on fair treatment of the outsider who comes in. The newcomer is not to be exploited by those already established.

The God of Israel attends to the afflicted whom others despise. This conviction runs through the Psalms (Psalm 9:12; 34:6) and shapes the Magnificat's praise of the God who lifts the lowly (Luke 1:52).

The king who judges the nations is the king whose scepter serves justice. Psalm 72 describes the same royal judging as defense of the poor and the needy (Psalm 72:2-4); the violence of verse 6 is aimed at the powers that oppress, the kings and rulers.

Judging by appearance is how the powerful win: the rich look credible and the poor do not. A king who sees past appearances, as God does when he looks on the heart (1 Samuel 16:7), is the only kind of judge the poor can trust. John 7:24 has Jesus warn against judging by appearance.

The Servant dies through a perversion of justice, arrested and sentenced and taken away. The chapter places God's saving work inside an unjust trial, which the Gospels narrate in detail. God's purpose in the Servant does not make the injustice just; it overrules it.

God takes the side of a humiliated people against those who mock them. The reversal promised here, the mockers bearing reproach and the mocked restored, is a pattern Scripture carries forward to Mary's song (Luke 1:51-53).

The judgment given ‘for’ the saints means God takes the side of the oppressed in his court. The biblical picture of God as the judge who vindicates the defenseless (Psalm 82:3-4) is applied here to a persecuted people.
The command to give and lend echoes Deuteronomy 15:7-11, where Israel is told to open its hand to the needy. Generosity to those in need is part of the righteousness that exceeds that of the scribes.

Giving to the poor is treated as an expected part of discipleship, in line with the law's command to open the hand to the needy (Deuteronomy 15:7-11). Jesus' concern is that the poor not be turned into props for the giver's reputation.
The Spirit's first effects in Acts include material generosity. Care for the needy is not an optional outgrowth of the church but part of its common life from the beginning.
